title: Continuous Token Flow Regulator and Kernel Prober
creator: Priya Desai
description:
Problem: We observe recurring p99 tail spikes (~3-6x over p95) for mixed workload clusters due to two interacting causes: (1) microbursts of short-prefill requests that never coalesce into efficient compute shapes, and (2) kernel mismatch where the runtime selects a generic kernel path suboptimal for the small/balanced sequence lengths. Current admission heuristics are brittle across tenant mixes and fail to maintain predictable latency when attention window drift occurs during multi-turn sessions.

Proposed solution: Implement a Continuous Token Flow Regulator (CTFR) combined with a lightweight Kernel Prober. CTFR is a tenant-aware pacing/filter that shapes the instantaneous token admission rate over a sliding window, smoothing microbursts while preserving tail SLOs for high-priority requests. The Kernel Prober periodically runs short, low-cost synthetic probes (no-op prompts) to measure effective per-token kernels across typical sequence-length quantiles and attention window sizes; these probes update a kernel affinity table used by the scheduler at admission time.

Key components:
- Token Flow Regulator: per-tenant leaky-bucket with adaptive leak rate computed from recent queue depth, observed decode latency, and tenant SLA tier. Supports priority preemption for emergency/interactive requests.
- Kernel Prober: non-customer probes scheduled at low priority; records kernel execution time for common shapes and quantizes results into affinity buckets (fast/slow/neutral). Probes are throttled to <0.1% capacity.
acceptance_criteria: p95 latency for mixed workloads remains within 1.2x baseline after rollout
p99 tail reduced by >=25% on testbed microburst scenarios
no increase in average token cost by more than 5% at global level
kernel affinity table maintained with <=5s staleness in steady-state
canary rollout (5% -> 25% -> 100%) shows no customer error-rate regression
technical_notes: Admission decision now consults three signals: regressed per-tenant leak rate, kernel affinity score, and attention-window estimator

Attention optimization: estimate 'effective attention length' on prefill by sampling token distributions in the first 8 tokens and biasing kernel selection toward attention-tiling kernels when < 512 tokens are likely
We will implement kernel affinity lookup as a small in-memory cache keyed by (model-variant, seq-length-bucket, attention-bucket) to avoid slow path costs during admission
Prober payloads are synthetic single-token prompts that emulate shaping but return quickly; probes are excluded from billing and metrics used for customer SLAs
rollout_plan: Feature gated behind runtime flag `ctfr_v1` and `kernel_prober_v1`
Stage 1 (lab): run on internal perf clusters with synthetic microburst harness (3 days)
Stage 2 (canary): enable for 5% of hosted traffic, monitor p95/p99, error rates, and cost (72h)
Stage 3 (expanded): 25% for 7 days, collect cold-start behavior and cross-tenant interactions
Stage 4: full rollout with automatic rollback if p99 increases over threshold
testing_plan: Unit tests for regulator calculations and leak-rate convergence
Load tests with mixed short/long sequence traces (derived from production trace anonymized set)
A/B runs comparing kernel selection with and without prober feedback
Chaos test: simulate lost probes and delayed affinity updates to validate graceful degradation
performance_targets: p99 improvement >= 25% in mixed microburst scenarios
KV cache and batching efficiency maintained (no >8% reduction in tokens/batch)
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Prober load interferes with real traffic; Mitigation: set strict quota and run probes at lowest priority on underutilized slots
Risk: Regulator over-throttles interactive workloads; Mitigation: priority bypass keys and short trial windows per tenant to learn safe leak rates
Risk: Kernel affinity staleness on model upgrades; Mitigation: invalidate affinity cache on model-variant or runtime-ABI change and run accelerated probing post-deploy
